If you read more than everyone else, you'll be better informed than everyone else. And it's cumulative. You can up your efficiency by scanning a wider range of relevant blogs and news feeds. And finally, 6 be thoughtful about your information sources and reduce redundancy. There's a major surplus of Finance information and Analysis at there when I went to work at a hedge fund, after my employer Lehman Brothers, went under, I had 20 Banks covering me at first, there was so much redundancy and useless information. I quickly narrowed my list down to 5 Banks and found that was much more manageable. How many overnight summaries does 1 person need There's plenty of good research on Wall Street, but there's also plenty of fluff. Get to know the strategists and researchers out there. Read the best and filter the rest. A few hundred good, Twitter follows are better than a few thousand, you'll find as you expand your media consumption, you get more and more redundant information nonsense. And cut and paste headlines that just waste your time. If you work at a hedge fund or institution, my estimate is you hit diminishing returns at about 3 to 5 coverage Banks? After that, the duplication is probably not worth the odd bit of unique analysis that squeaks through The philosophy be curious, keep learning and build knowledge for the long run. Cognitive trait. Number 3 is quantitative. many trading roles require in-depth knowledge of statistics, and the ability to code or program usually in Python Even a Trader in the most vanilla discretionary or short-term trading seat benefits from quantitative sophistication. I'll love numeracy under this heading as well, because the ability to intuitively understand numbers helps Traders enormously. For example, many Market, making roles require quick calculations converting Yen to Dollars when a salesperson asks, for a price in a fast market. For example. Traders that can do quick, Mental Math have a small advantage over. Those that cannot here's how to level up your quantitative skills. 1, learn about expected value and decision trees. These are specially useful when trading economic or Market events with discrete outcomes for example. You think the FED will cut rates today and the market has it priced as 80% 20% in favor of a rate cut. A professional rates Trader might say that, 20 out of 25 basis points are priced in. You decide to risk. 200,000 on the trade, you'll make 50,000. If you're correct and the FED Cuts rates, if they don't cut you, lose your thousand dollars. Many people will see this negative leverage as bad, you risking 200 to make just 50 but it is not inherently good or bad. It depends on the probabilities, you assigned to each outcome. The tricky thing with Market probabilities, is that unlike probabilities in gambling, they are not known. Or measurable you have to estimate them. Accurately. Estimating, probabilities is a skill. That gives you an edge in trading. Incomplete information is 1 of the challenging Hallmarks of markets as an exercise in probability. Now going back to our example, let's say, you think there's a 95% chance. The FED will cut rates in the PDF. I show the expected value of a 200,000 wager on that event. And you can see in the PDF that even though your risking 200 to make 50. It's still an excellent trade idea. Clearly though, your confidence in that 95% figure is key to making this bet. If you think it's more like 70 or 80% then stay away, your view is about the same as the market. I assume that most people listening to this book, have a pretty clear understanding of expected value. But if you're new to the game or you are sick the day, this was taught in University. Statistics brush up go online and take a short course or do some Reading about expected value. Good Traders work.
